components.name: Guest web app
components.responsibility: Shows available tables and lets a guest hold one.
components.example: The booking form disables itself the moment it is submitted, so an impatient double-click cannot create two holds.

depth.simple: The website a guest uses. It shows which tables are free and sends the booking request onward.
depth.balanced: A Next.js app rendering the availability grid and booking form. It never decides whether a table is free — it asks the API and renders the answer.
depth.deep: Availability is fetched per service window and revalidated on focus. The optimistic hold in `useReservation` is display-only; the authoritative answer always arrives from the API, and a 409 rolls the optimistic state back.

why.q: Why does it not check availability itself?
why.a: Two guests can hold conflicting state in two browsers at the same time. Only the database sees both requests, so only the database can decide.

components.name: Reservations API
components.responsibility: Accepts reservation requests and enforces table availability.
components.example: POST /api/reservations with a table id and time window returns 409 when the slot is already held.

depth.simple: The part that decides whether a booking is allowed.
depth.balanced: A Fastify service exposing the reservation routes. It validates the request shape, then delegates the actual conflict decision to the database constraint.
depth.deep: Routes are registered in `routes/index.ts`; each handler is thin. `placeReservation` opens a transaction, inserts, and translates a unique-violation into a 409 rather than a 500 — the distinction matters because the client retries one and not the other.

why.q: Why is the conflict check not in the handler?
why.a: A check-then-insert in application code leaves a window between the two statements. The constraint closes it.

changed.note: Now returns 409 instead of 500 on conflict

components.name: Availability engine
components.responsibility: Turns opening hours, turn times, and existing bookings into bookable slots.
components.example: A 90-minute turn time on a 6pm–10pm service produces slots at 18:00, 19:30, and 21:00 — not a continuous range.

depth.simple: The rules that decide which times a guest is allowed to pick.
depth.balanced: A pure package with no database access. It receives opening hours, turn times, and existing reservations and returns a slot grid. Being pure is what makes it testable against timezone edge cases.
depth.deep: `computeSlots` expands opening hours into intervals, subtracts held ranges, and snaps to the turn-time lattice. DST transitions are handled by computing in UTC and rendering in the venue timezone; the boundary case is pinned by `dst.spec.ts`.

why.q: Why is this a separate package rather than part of the API?
why.a: The nightly worker and the API both need identical slot maths. Duplicating it once produced a mismatch between what guests saw and what the API accepted.

components.name: Postgres
components.responsibility: Stores venues, tables, reservations, and the overlap constraint that arbitrates conflicts.
components.example: An exclusion constraint on (table_id, time_range) rejects the second of two overlapping inserts.

depth.simple: Where everything is remembered — and the referee for who got the table.
depth.balanced: Postgres with an exclusion constraint over a time range per table. The constraint is the single point where two racing requests meet, which is why the API can stay simple.
depth.deep: `0007_reservation_overlap.sql` adds `EXCLUDE USING gist (table_id WITH =, during WITH &&) WHERE (status = 'confirmed')`. Cancelled rows are excluded from the constraint so a cancellation frees the slot without a delete.

why.q: What would break if the constraint were removed?
why.a: Nothing, until two requests arrive in the same millisecond. Then both succeed and one guest arrives to a taken table.

components.name: Nightly worker
components.responsibility: Rebuilds the availability cache and expires abandoned holds.
components.example: A hold that was never confirmed within 15 minutes is released at the next sweep.

depth.simple: A background program that tidies up overnight.
depth.balanced: A scheduled process running two jobs: rebuilding the cached slot grid per venue, and expiring stale holds. It shares the availability package with the API so both agree.
depth.deep: Jobs are idempotent and safe to re-run; each takes an advisory lock keyed by venue so two workers never rebuild the same venue concurrently.

why.q: Why is expiry not handled by a database TTL?
why.a: Postgres has no row TTL, and expiry must also publish an event so connected clients refresh.

connections.label: submits reservation requests
connections.data: Table id, time window, party size
connections.validation: Zod schema at the route boundary
connections.auth: Session cookie verified in middleware before the handler runs
connections.onSuccess: 201 with the confirmed reservation; the grid refetches
connections.onFailure: 409 when the slot was taken between render and submit; the form shows the next free time
connections.retry: None — the client refetches availability instead of retrying blindly
connections.recovery: Availability is refetched on window focus
connections.whyThisMechanism: A plain request/response fits an action the guest is waiting on.

connections.label: reads and writes reservations
connections.validation: CHECK constraints and the overlap exclusion
connections.auth: Connection-level role; row-level security scopes rows to the venue
connections.whyThisMechanism: The database is the only place two racing requests are both visible.

connections.label: asks which slots exist
connections.data: Opening hours, turn time, existing bookings
connections.onFailure: Throws on an invalid service window; surfaces as 500
connections.whyThisMechanism: Pure in-process call; no need for a network hop for deterministic maths.

connections.label: expires abandoned holds
connections.onFailure: Job retried on the next tick; advisory lock prevents overlap
connections.whyThisMechanism: Expiry is not urgent and must not compete with guest traffic.

workflows.title: A guest reserves a table
workflows.hook: This is where a tap on a button becomes a row that nobody else can take.
workflows.trigger: Guest presses Reserve in the booking form
workflows.outcome: A confirmed reservation and an updated availability grid
workflows.recap: The interface is optimistic, the API is careful, and the database is the referee. Every layer assumes the one below it might say no.

steps.title: The form submits
steps.plain: The booking form disables itself and posts the chosen table and time to the API.
steps.why: Disabling first is what stops an impatient double-click from creating two holds.
steps.input: Table id, start time, party size
steps.failure: Offline or 5xx — an inline error appears, the form re-enables, and nothing was written.

excerpt.caption: The guard that prevents a second POST

steps.title: The request is validated
steps.plain: The API checks that the request has the right shape before doing anything else.
steps.why: Shape validation keeps malformed input out of the domain, so every layer below can assume well-formed data.
steps.failure: 400 with the offending field. Nothing reaches the database.

steps.title: The session is checked
steps.plain: Middleware confirms the guest has a session before the handler runs.
steps.why: The frontend already hides the form from signed-out guests, but that is a convenience. This is the boundary.
steps.output: The authenticated guest id on the request
steps.failure: 401. The response does not reveal whether the table exists.

steps.title: The row is inserted
steps.plain: The API opens a transaction and inserts the reservation. The database decides whether it is allowed.
steps.why: Checking first and inserting second leaves a gap. Letting the constraint decide removes the gap entirely.
steps.input: A typed reservation request and the guest id
steps.failure: An exclusion violation means someone else won the race — translated to 409, not 500.

excerpt.caption: A conflict is an expected outcome, not an error

steps.title: The grid updates
steps.plain: The form clears, the reservation appears, and the availability grid refetches so the slot disappears for everyone else.
steps.why: Refetching rather than patching local state keeps what the guest sees identical to what the API would say.
steps.failure: If the refetch fails the confirmation still shows — the reservation exists regardless of what the grid renders.

failureScenario.title: Two guests, one table
steps: Both browsers render the same free slot.
Both post within the same second.
The second violates the exclusion constraint.
The API answers 409 with the next free time.
failureScenario.resolution: The second guest sees a specific alternative rather than a generic error.

entities.name: Reservation
entities.realWorldMeaning: A promise that a specific table is held for a specific guest at a specific time.

relationships.note: A table has many reservations over time

entities.whySeparate: Split from Order because a reservation exists before anything is charged, and survives a cancelled order.

depth.simple: A table held for someone at a time.
depth.balanced: The central operational row. Its `during` time range participates in the exclusion constraint, which is what makes double-booking impossible.
depth.deep: Only rows with `status = 'confirmed'` participate in the constraint, so cancelling frees a slot without deleting history. `held` rows carry an expiry the nightly worker sweeps.

why.q: Why keep cancelled rows at all?
why.a: No-show rate per guest is computed from them, and deleting would lose the audit trail of who cancelled when.

entities.name: Table
entities.realWorldMeaning: A physical table with a seat count, in a venue.
entities.whySeparate: Tables change rarely and reservations change constantly — separating them keeps the hot table small.

depth.balanced: Configuration data, edited by staff and read on nearly every request. It is retired rather than deleted so historical reservations keep resolving.
depth.deep: Retiring sets `retired_at`; the availability engine filters on it at slot-computation time rather than at query time, so past bookings still render.

why.a: Deleting would orphan every historical reservation that references it.

failureScenario.title: The slot was taken a moment ago
steps: API answers 409 with the next free time
failureScenario.recovery: The form offers the alternative directly rather than asking the guest to look again.

depth.simple: The website asking the server to do something and waiting for the answer.
depth.balanced: Plain HTTP request/response over JSON, authenticated by a session cookie and validated at the route boundary.
depth.deep: Errors are deliberately split: 4xx means the guest can act on it, 5xx means retry is pointless. The client only retries the latter, and never the 409.

why.q: Why is a conflict a 409 rather than a 500?
why.a: A conflict is an expected outcome of a busy restaurant, not a fault. The client shows an alternative rather than an error.

auth.identity: Email and password, verified against a bcrypt hash.
auth.sessionModel: Signed HTTP-only cookie carrying a session id; sessions live in Redis with a 14-day TTL.

enforcementPoints.what: Admin routes redirect when no session cookie is present
enforcementPoints.note: Convenience only. Anyone can call the API directly, so this is never the security boundary.

enforcementPoints.what: Every admin handler re-checks the staff role
Row-level security scopes every row to the caller's venue

roles.name: guest
roles.grants: Create and cancel their own reservations

roles.name: staff
roles.grants: Read and update reservations for their venue

roles.name: owner
roles.grants: Everything staff can do, plus managing tables and staff

auth.failureBehaviour: 401 for missing identity, 403 for insufficient role. Neither reveals whether the resource exists.
auth.whyMultipleLayers: The frontend check is for user experience. The backend check is the boundary. Row-level security is the backstop for the day a query forgets its venue filter.

depth.simple: How the system knows who you are, and what that lets you do.
depth.balanced: Session-cookie authentication with role checks in middleware and row-level security in the database. Identity and permission are separate questions answered in separate places.
depth.deep: Sessions are rotated on privilege change so an in-flight session cannot retain a revoked role. RLS policies are venue-scoped and applied even to the service role in the admin path.

why.q: Why is the same thing checked three times?
why.a: Each layer protects against a different failure: a confusing UI, a missing handler check, and a forgotten WHERE clause.

subsystems.name: Availability engine
subsystems.hook: At first this looks like an over-engineered calendar. Then the clocks go back an hour and it earns every line.
subsystems.purpose: Turn opening hours, turn times, and existing bookings into the exact list of times a guest may pick.
subsystems.inputs: Venue opening hours, turn time, table list, confirmed reservations
subsystems.outputs: A slot grid per table per service

stages.name: Expand opening hours
stages.what: Service windows become concrete UTC intervals for the requested date.

stages.name: Subtract held ranges
stages.what: Confirmed reservations are removed from each table's interval.

stages.name: Snap to turn time
stages.what: Remaining space is quantised to the turn-time lattice so slots line up across tables.

dataStructures.name: SlotGrid
dataStructures.what: Table id to an ordered list of start times.

invariants: A table never has two overlapping confirmed reservations.
Slot starts always align to the turn-time lattice.
subsystems.whyDesignedThisWay: Keeping the package pure means both the API and the worker can run it and always agree.
subsystems.connectionToSystem: Called in-process by the API for every availability request and by the worker during the nightly rebuild.
failurePoints: DST transitions shift slot edges if computation leaves UTC.
A venue with a turn time longer than its service window produces an empty grid.

startHere.advice: Start at computeSlots. Everything else feeds it, and the tests around it describe the edge cases better than any comment.

depth.simple: The part that works out which times you are allowed to choose.
depth.balanced: A pure package with three stages: expand hours, subtract bookings, snap to the turn-time lattice. No database access, which is what makes its timezone behaviour testable.
depth.deep: All arithmetic happens in UTC; venue-local rendering is the last step. The DST test fixes a 25-hour day and asserts the slot count, which is the only reliable way to catch an off-by-one hour.

why.q: Why not compute slots in SQL?
why.a: The turn-time lattice needs branching that reads poorly in SQL, and the same logic is needed in the worker where no request context exists.

testTypes.name: Unit
testTypes.covers: Availability maths and domain rules in isolation
testTypes.why: The slot lattice breaks silently; unit tests are the only fast way to notice.

testTypes.name: Integration
testTypes.covers: API routes against a real Postgres
testTypes.why: The conflict behaviour lives in a database constraint, so it cannot be tested with a mock.

testTypes.name: Browser
testTypes.covers: The booking flow end to end
testTypes.why: Double-submit protection is a UI behaviour and only reproduces in a real browser.

manualChecks: Book across a DST boundary on staging before a release that touches availability.

environment.testDatabase: Ephemeral Postgres container per run, migrated from scratch

delivery.debugging: Set LOG_LEVEL=debug to see the constraint violation before it is translated to a 409.
traps: Migrations must be regenerated after a schema edit or CI fails at the drift check.
The e2e suite needs the worker running; `pnpm dev` starts it, a bare `next dev` does not.
delivery.release: Tagging on master triggers the deploy workflow; migrations run before the new image receives traffic.
delivery.whyTheseLayers: Each layer catches a class the previous one cannot see: types catch shape, unit tests catch maths, integration tests catch the database contract, browser tests catch the interface.

depth.simple: How a change gets checked before real guests see it.
depth.balanced: Four verification layers run locally and again in CI, then a tag on master deploys with migrations first.
depth.deep: The drift check compares generated migrations against the schema snapshot; it is the most common CI failure and almost always means a forgotten regeneration.

startHere.advice: Create a new numbered migration. Never edit one that has been applied.

alsoAffects.what: Add it to the type if the engine needs it
Collect it if a guest supplies it

projectInstructions.rule: Every migration needs a matching down migration.

doNotTouch.why: Regenerated by the build; edits are lost.

changePlaybooks.whyHere: The schema is the source of truth for every layer above it, so it changes first and the rest follows.

startHere.advice: Copy the shape of reservations.ts — thin handler, schema at the boundary, domain call inside.

changePlaybooks.whyHere: Routes stay thin so the interesting logic remains testable without HTTP.

glossary.technical: The unit of restaurant capacity. A party of four consumes four covers.
glossary.why: Capacity is limited by seats rather than tables, so every limit in the system is expressed in covers.
glossary.example: A 40-cover dining room can seat ten parties of four.

glossary.short: How long a table is held for one booking.
glossary.technical: The quantisation interval for the slot lattice; 90 minutes by default, configurable per venue.
glossary.why: Without a fixed turn time, slots would not line up across tables and the grid would be unreadable.
glossary.example: A 90-minute turn time on a 6pm–10pm service yields slots at 18:00, 19:30, and 21:00.

knowledgeChecks.question: Two guests submit for the same table in the same second. Which part of the system decides who wins?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Only the database sees both requests. The form prevents one guest double-submitting, and the availability engine never touches live rows — so the constraint is the only place the race is visible.

groups.whyItMatters: This is where every guest-facing reservation workflow begins and ends.

groups.whyItMatters: This boundary validates requests and translates database decisions into responses.

openQuestions.question: Why is the hold expiry exactly 15 minutes?
openQuestions.whatIsKnown: services/worker/src/jobs/expireHolds.ts uses a 15-minute threshold with no comment.
openQuestions.whyUnknown: No test, comment, or commit message explains the number.
openQuestions.whereToLook: The operations team, or the original booking-flow design discussion.

readingOrder.hook: Six files, in the order that makes each one explain the next. Nothing here is locked — an arrow says what a file assumes you already know, not what you are allowed to open.
readingOrder.goal: Read the reservation path once, in an order where every file is explained by the ones before it, and finish able to say which layer actually prevents a double booking.

nodes.title: README.md
nodes.what: What the product is, how to run it, and what each environment variable is for.
nodes.lookFor: The availability model described in prose — you will meet it again as a database constraint.
nodes.validate: Bring the stack up and make one reservation by hand. Everything below has a running system behind it.

nodes.title: 0007_reservation_overlap.sql
nodes.what: The exclusion constraint that makes two overlapping confirmed reservations unrepresentable.
nodes.lookFor: That the guarantee is here, in the schema — not in the service that produces the friendly 409.
nodes.validate: Insert two overlapping rows directly in psql. The database should refuse before any application code runs.

nodes.title: db/reservations.ts
nodes.what: Every read and write of a reservation, and the only place the audit row is guaranteed alongside it.
nodes.lookFor: That the constraint violation is caught here and translated, rather than being prevented here.
nodes.validate: Find the error code it maps to a 409, and check it against the constraint name in the migration.

nodes.title: BookingForm.tsx
nodes.what: Where a tap becomes a request, and where a double submission is stopped.
nodes.lookFor: The pending guard before the POST. It prevents one guest racing themselves, not two guests racing each other.
nodes.validate: test/e2e/booking.spec.ts — the "double submit" case is the one to read.

nodes.title: useReservation.ts
nodes.what: The optimistic update, and what it does when the server disagrees.
nodes.lookFor: How a 409 is distinguished from a network failure — they look identical to a naive catch and mean opposite things.
nodes.validate: Take the API down and then make the API return 409. The two should not produce the same message.

nodes.title: availability/index.ts
nodes.what: The slot grid the booking UI renders, computed rather than stored.
nodes.lookFor: Why it is recomputed rather than cached: a stale grid shows a slot that the constraint will then refuse.
nodes.validate: Move the clock across a DST boundary and check the slot edges.
